title: New every morning (Lamentations 3:22–23)
hook: in the middle of the lament: God's mercies "are new every morning"

segments.voice: Yesterday, eichah: Lamentations opened on a city sitting alone, tears on her cheeks. Today, a light comes on in the middle of that book.

Halfway through Lamentations, a man speaks from what feels like the bottom of a pit. He's been led into darkness, he says, hedged in so he can't get out, his prayers shut out. Line after line, it gets heavier. Then, with no warning, one sentence changes direction: "This I recall to my mind, Therefore have I hope." Nothing outside him has changed. The city is still in ruins. What changes is what he chooses to remember.
screen: `A VOICE FROM THE BOTTOM OF A PIT.` → `THIS I RECALL TO MY MIND.` → `NOTHING OUTSIDE HAS CHANGED.`

segments.voice: New every morning. Here's what he recalls, in the JPS 1917 translation: "Surely the LORD's mercies are not consumed, Surely His compassions fail not. They are new every morning; Great is Thy faithfulness." Two words carry the weight. Mercies, in Hebrew chasadim: steady, loyal kindness, the kind that keeps a promise. Compassions, rachamim: tenderness, the way a parent feels toward a child. Those, he says, don't run out. They aren't stored up once, like grain in a barn, to be rationed until they're gone. They arrive fresh, a little like the manna in the wilderness, which came each morning and couldn't be saved for later. Then he adds: "The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; Therefore will I hope in Him." Now notice where this sits. Not at the end of the book, as a happy ending. Right in the middle. The chapters before it mourn; the chapters after it mourn again. The hope doesn't erase the lament; the lament surrounds it on both sides. It's an honest shape for hope: not a door out of sorrow, but a lamp lit inside it. And the claim is small and daily. Not, everything is fine. Just: this morning, something was given that wasn't there last night. The phrase has traveled into the start of the Jewish day. Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, thanks God for returning the soul, and ends with these words: rabbah emunatecha, great is your faithfulness. A line from the ruins, said at dawn.
screen: `MERCIES AND COMPASSIONS FAIL NOT.` · `GIVEN FRESH, NOT STORED UP.` · then, large: `HOPE IN THE MIDDLE OF THE LAMENT.` · then: `GREAT IS THY FAITHFULNESS, AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Go back over the hours since you woke and find one thing given to you today that you didn't earn or plan: light through a window, a kind word, a body that got out of bed, a cup of something warm. Hold that one thing for a moment, the way the voice in the pit held one memory. If you pray, you can say the old words: great is thy faithfulness.
Modeh Ani, the short prayer said on waking, which thanks God for a new day and ends with Lamentations' words: great is your faithfulness. Today's word.
Your line: a lamp lit inside it. Hope, right in the middle of the lament. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: How can a book of mourning like Lamentations talk about hope?
options: Its hope sits in the middle of the lament, small and daily: mercies new every morning.
The hope comes at the very end, a happy ending that erases all the sorrow before it.
It says the ruins weren't truly sad, since God's mercies mean nothing was really lost.
chat.meaning: Lamentations sets 'new every morning' in its middle chapter, with mourning on both sides: not a door out of sorrow, a lamp inside it.
